elements.quote: Diabetes is a major cause of death and disability around the world and is projected to increase in the coming decades (1)... The prevalence of type 2 diabetes and its risk factors are strongly associated with underlying social and economic factors (2)... Sobers-Grannum and colleagues examined the effects of gender on diabetes, its risk factors, and outcomes in the Caribbean in a systematic review published in 2015 (4). In addition to gender, the review sought to describe data on a range of social determinants of health, but evidence was scant, making it impossible to provide even a narrative review of the relationship of outcomes to other social determinants.
elements.reason: The introduction describes the current state of knowledge (global diabetes burden, association with social determinants, prior Caribbean review findings) and explicitly identifies the uncertainty that evidence on social determinants other than gender was scant.

elements.quote: The objective of this review was to inform policy agenda-setting for diabetes prevention and control in the Caribbean, and to identify gaps in the evidence where further research is needed.
elements.reason: The importance and need for the review are clearly explained: to inform policy agenda-setting for diabetes prevention/control in the Caribbean and to identify evidence gaps, addressing the scant evidence on social determinants beyond gender.

elements.quote: Sobers-Grannum and colleagues examined the effects of gender on diabetes, its risk factors, and outcomes in the Caribbean in a systematic review published in 2015 (4)... the present study updates the previous systematic review (4) with new data, including new information on physical activity, a wider range of social determinants, and sources from the grey literature.
elements.reason: A previous similar systematic review is identified and cited (Sobers-Grannum et al., 2015, reference 4), and the need for the current review is explained as an update adding new data, more social determinants, and grey literature.

This is a review of observational studies on the distribution of diabetes and risk factors by social determinants, not a review of intervention effects, so no mechanism of action needs to be described.

The review examines associations between social determinants and diabetes outcomes in observational studies, not a complex intervention or delivery context, so a logic model of intervention components is not required.

elements.quote: Objectives. To conduct an analysis of the most recent data on diabetes and its risk factors by gender and other social determinants of health to understand why its prevalence is higher among women than men in the Caribbean; to inform policy agenda-setting for diabetes prevention and control in the Caribbean; and to identify gaps in the evidence that require further research.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states the review objectives, and the Introduction/Methods reiterate the objective and the framework guiding the determinants examined: 'Guided by the analytical framework recommended by the WHO Commission on the Social Determinants of Health (3)... The objective of this review was to inform policy agenda-setting for diabetes prevention and control in the Caribbean, and to identify gaps in the evidence where further research is needed.' Determinants were framed using the Progress-plus checklist (text_3).

This is a review of diabetes distribution, risk factors, and outcomes by social determinants (etiological/descriptive), not a review of intervention effects, so no planned intervention comparisons in PICO format are required.

elements.quote: Studies included had: Caribbean study population Adult participants ( ≥ 18 years of age) when considering diabetes and its outcomes, or participants ≥ 12 years when considering risk factors Outcomes stratified by at least one of the social determinants Quantitative study design (observational/intervention) Sample size ≥ 50 people
elements.reason: Eligibility criteria specify population, setting (Caribbean), age, study design, outcome stratification, and minimum sample size, plus outcomes of interest for general and diabetic populations.

elements.quote: Studies were included if the complete text was available; if not, they were excluded. There were no limits regarding the language of publication.
elements.reason: Report characteristics addressed: full-text availability requirement and explicit statement of no language limits; date range (2007–2016) also specified.
The review does not distinguish exclusion for outcomes not measured versus outcomes measured but results not reported; exclusion reasons in the flowchart are generic (e.g., 'Other reasons: 142').

elements.quote: Only population-based, cross-­ sectional studies that measured the outcomes as dichotomous variables were included for meta-analysis... Other social determinants were too heterogeneously defined to allow for meta-analysis; these were described narratively. Measures were included in the narrative review when at least four relationships from multiple studies were available.
elements.reason: Synthesis grouping is specified: meta-analysis of gender comparisons for dichotomous outcomes in population-based cross-sectional studies, narrative synthesis for other social determinants, with thresholds for inclusion.

elements.quote: Search criteria were deliberately kept broad so as to capture any relationship related to diabetes and one of the social determinants.
elements.reason: A rationale is given for broad search criteria, but rationales for other notable restrictions (e.g., sample size ≥ 50, full-text availability) are not provided.

No date on which any database, register, or website was last searched is reported anywhere in the retrieved evidence; only the coverage period of included data (1 January 2007 - 31 December 2016) is given, which is not a search date.

elements.quote: A systematic search was conducted of PubMed Central (U.S. National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, Maryland, United States); EMBASE (Excerpta Medica Database, Elsevier, Amsterdam, the Netherlands); the Virtual Health Library, including LILACS (Latin American and Caribbean Center on Health Sciences Information, PAHO/WHO, São Paolo, Brazil; BIREME); MedCarib (Health sciences data from the English speaking Caribbean; BIREME); and IBECS (Biographic Index on Health Sciences; BIREME).
elements.reason: Database names and platforms/providers are reported, but no coverage dates or date of last search are given for any database.

elements.quote: Reports from the WHO STEP-wise approach to noncommunicable disease risk factor surveillance surveys (STEPS; 7) and other nationally representative NCD reports were identified from PAHO (8)
elements.reason: The STEPS surveillance reports and PAHO/WHO repositories are named as sources, but no date restrictions or consultation dates are reported.

elements.quote: added newer data collected from NCD survey reports available on the websites of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) and WHO
elements.reason: The PAHO and WHO websites are named as online sources consulted, but no URLs or search/consultation dates are provided.
No organisations or manufacturers contacted to identify studies are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No types of individuals contacted to identify studies are described in the retrieved evidence.
No examination of reference lists is reported in the retrieved evidence.
No backward or forward citation searching is reported in the retrieved evidence.
No journals or conference proceedings consulted directly are reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: using the same search strategies as the original (4), this review included data for three additional years (2014 - 2016), extending the collection from 1 January 2007 - 31 December 2016... A systematic search was conducted of PubMed Central...; EMBASE...; the Virtual Health Library, including LILACS...; MedCarib...; and IBECS... Reports from the WHO STEP-wise approach... were identified from PAHO
elements.reason: All databases and websites searched are named, but the actual full search strings are not reproduced; the paper only refers to the strategies of the original review (reference 4), so the complete search strategy as run is not reported.

elements.quote: this review included data for three additional years (2014 - 2016), extending the collection from 1 January 2007 - 31 December 2016. A search was conducted for studies in the Caribbean-its countries and territories as defined by Samuels and colleagues (5)
elements.reason: Date limits and the Caribbean geographic scope are stated and tied to eligibility (Caribbean studies, 2007-2016), but other potential limits/filters (e.g., language, publication type) are not described or justified.

elements.quote: The study protocol for this review followed that of Sobers-­ Grannum and colleagues (4) and added newer data collected from NCD survey reports available on the websites of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) and WHO.
elements.reason: A published search approach (Sobers-Grannum et al.) is cited and reused, and the addition of PAHO/WHO website sources is noted, but specific adaptations to the search strings/filters themselves are not described.
No evidence that natural-language processing or text-analysis tools were used to identify or refine search terms.
No evidence that tools were used to translate search strings between sources; strategies were reused from the original review.
No validation of the search strategy is reported in the retrieved evidence.
No peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) is reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Guided by the Progress-plus checklist (6), the social determinants examined were: gender; marital status; income; housing; urban/rural location;
elements.reason: The search structure was based on an existing framework (Progress-plus) and a prior published review, so the conditional requirement to describe a non-PICO conceptual structure developed de novo does not apply.

elements.quote: Titles and abstracts were independently reviewed by two reviewers (LG and CB); conflicts were resolved by a third reviewer (NS). The full text of all retained articles was sought, and where available, was independently abstracted by two reviewers (LG and CB); again, any differences were resolved in discussion with a third reviewer (NS).
elements.reason: Two reviewers screened titles/abstracts and two reviewers handled full texts; the number of reviewers at each stage is specified.

elements.quote: Titles and abstracts were independently reviewed by two reviewers (LG and CB)

No evidence of processes for obtaining eligibility information from study investigators; no indication this occurred.

elements.quote: There were no limits regarding the language of publication.
elements.reason: No translation methods reported; no evidence that non-English records required translation for eligibility assessment.

elements.quote: Bibliographic information for each study was entered into the Rayyan online data system (Qatar Computing Research Institute, Doha, Qatar; 10).

No externally derived classifiers were reported.
No internally derived classifiers were reported.
No machine-learning prioritisation or stopping rules reported.
No crowdsourcing platforms used or reported.
No previously screened datasets used to eliminate records were reported.

elements.quote: The full text of all retained articles was sought, and where available, was independently abstracted by two reviewers (LG and CB)
elements.reason: States that two reviewers abstracted data from each report.

elements.quote: was independently abstracted by two reviewers (LG and CB)
elements.reason: Explicitly reports that the two data abstractors worked independently.

elements.quote: again, any differences were resolved in discussion with a third reviewer (NS)
elements.reason: Describes the process for resolving disagreements during data abstraction via a third reviewer.
No evidence of any process for obtaining or confirming data from study investigators.
No automation tools were reported for data collection; the manuscript describes only manual abstraction with a custom form, so no automation tool reporting applies.

elements.quote: There were no limits regarding the language of publication.
elements.reason: No translation methods for data collection are described; nothing indicates non-English articles required translation, so the requirement does not apply based on reported evidence.
No mention of extracting data from figures; data were abstracted using a form, so figure-extraction software does not apply.

elements.quote: It was possible to have more than one paper published for a study.
elements.reason: The manuscript acknowledges multiple reports per study and analysis was done at relationship level, but no explicit decision rules for selecting data among multiple reports or resolving inconsistencies are described.

elements.quote: For the general population, the review looked at: obesity, including measures of body mass index (BMI), waist circumference (WC), and abdominal obesity; physical inactivity; tobacco use; measures of diet quality, e.g., consumption of fruits and vegetables, diet quality scores, etc.; and type 1 and type 2 diabetes prevalence and incidence. Among those with diabetes, the review considered: control measures, including glucose, glycated hemoglobin, blood pressure, and lipids; measures of incidence or prevalence of retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, diabetic foot, and lower extremity amputation; and mortality.
elements.reason: The methods explicitly list the outcome domains sought in the general population and among people with diabetes, with definitions for some (e.g., obesity via BMI/WC/abdominal obesity); text_3 further defines physical inactivity dichotomously against WHO recommendations.

elements.quote: this review included data for three additional years (2014 - 2016), extending the collection from 1 January 2007 - 31 December 2016.
elements.reason: The date range refers to publication/source inclusion period, not the time frame or time points of outcome measurement within studies. No measurement time points for outcomes are specified.

elements.quote: Search criteria were deliberately kept broad so as to capture any relationship related to diabetes and one of the social determinants.
elements.reason: The breadth of the search suggests all compatible relationships were sought, but the manuscript does not explicitly state whether all compatible results (all measures, time points, analyses) within each outcome domain were collected.

elements.quote: Measures were included in the narrative review when at least four relationships from multiple studies were available.
elements.reason: A selection rule is described for which results were analysed (minimum of four relationships for narrative review; only dichotomous outcomes from population-based cross-sectional studies included in meta-analysis).

elements.quote: this review features WHO STEP surveys that are largely unpublished in peer reviewed journals.
elements.reason: Although the review is an update, no changes to outcome-domain definitions or importance during the review are reported with rationales.

elements.quote: The study protocol for this review followed that of Sobers-­ Grannum and colleagues (4)
elements.reason: No changes to the processes for selecting results within outcome domains are reported; only adherence to the prior protocol is mentioned.

elements.quote: To conduct an analysis of the most recent data on diabetes and its risk factors by gender and other social determinants of health to understand why its prevalence is higher among women than men in the Caribbean
elements.reason: Gender is implicitly the most important outcome-stratifying variable given the stated objective and the meta-analyses focus on gender contrasts, but no explicit statement prioritising outcomes for interpreting conclusions with a rationale is provided.

elements.quote: For the general population, the review looked at: obesity, including measures of body mass index (BMI), waist circumference (WC), and abdominal obesity; physical inactivity; tobacco use; measures of diet quality... elements.reason: The variables sought (outcomes and social determinants) are listed, and a few are defined (e.g., physical inactivity defined dichotomously in text_3), but most variables are not explicitly defined and no assumptions about missing/unclear information during abstraction are reported.

No retrieved text describes assumptions made about missing or unclear study information during data abstraction; risk-of-bias 'unclear' categories are mentioned but not assumptions for missing data items.

elements.quote: The form was guided by the STROBE statement (11) for reporting observational epidemiology and by the PRISMA statement on systematic reviews concerning health equality (12).
elements.reason: The tools (STROBE and PRISMA-Equity) used to determine which data items to collect for the abstraction form are explicitly cited.

elements.quote: Risk of bias was assessed using criteria applied by Brown and colleagues (14) for each relationship and classified as follows
elements.reason: The risk-of-bias assessment tool is specified as the criteria applied by Brown and colleagues (reference 14).

elements.quote: Low risk of bias (all criteria are met)-response rate > 75%, missing data < 10%, full description of sampling strategy, adjustment of measures by age and other potential confounders (such as sex or ethnicity), as appropriate, and objective measurement of disease measures
elements.reason: The components assessed by the tool are detailed: response rate, missing data, sampling strategy description, confounder adjustment, and objective vs subjective measurement of disease measures.

elements.quote: Medium risk of bias (one or more criterion)-response rate 50% - 75%, missing data 10% - 15% ... High risk of bias (one or more criterion)-response rate ≤ 50%, missing data > 15% ... Unclear-not enough information to make an assessment.
elements.reason: An overall risk-of-b judgement (low/medium/high/unclear) was made and the rules for deriving each overall classification are explicitly reported.
No evidence describes any adaptation of the existing risk-of-bias criteria; the manuscript only states the criteria of Brown and colleagues were applied.
No newly developed risk-of-bias tool is reported in the retrieved evidence.

The manuscript reports two independent reviewers for screening and abstraction ('Titles and abstracts were independently reviewed by two reviewers (LG and CB)'), but does not state how many reviewers assessed risk of bias, whether independently, or how disagreements were resolved for the risk-of-bias assessment specifically.

elements.quote: Only population-based, cross-­ sectional studies that measured the outcomes as dichotomous variables were included for meta-analysis. Meta-analyses were conducted and random effects models were fitted...

No thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect sizes, nor their rationale, are reported anywhere in the retrieved evidence.
No description of methods to re-express synthesized results using another effect measure appears in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Only population-based, cross-­ sectional studies that measured the outcomes as dichotomous variables were included for meta-analysis. elements.quote: A full matrix of relationships of outcomes by social determinants is available in ­ Table 1.

No locations (e.g., repositories, links) for publicly available review materials such as forms, extracted data, or analytic code are reported. The PAHO/WHO website mentions refer to source data of included surveys, not to review outputs.
